# IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS

Giving a router an IPv6 address does not make its IPv4 IGP carry those prefixes. OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) is an IPv4 protocol. To run a link-state IGP for IPv6 you either start a **different protocol**, **OSPFv3**, or you teach **IS-IS** — which can already carry more than one address family in one process — to advertise IPv6 reachability. This chapter is the IPv6 IGP note: what is actually different, how FRR names the knobs, and when a single IS-IS process with multi-topology is a better fit than “OSPFv2 plus OSPFv3.”

It is not a second OSPF basics chapter, and it is not a second IS-IS basics chapter. Those already cover areas, costs, NETs, levels, and DIS. A later lab-host track runs IPv6 and IS-IS on cEOS and FRR; this chapter is the conceptual and config-shape layer those labs assume. Address assignment (SLAAC, RA flags, DHCPv6) is a different chapter and is not retold here.

## Learning goals

- Explain why OSPFv3 is not “OSPFv2 with IPv6 addresses,” including the 32-bit router ID, link-local hellos, and where prefixes actually travel
- Configure a minimal FRR `router ospf6` and a minimal dual-stack IS-IS (RFC 5308 TLVs, `ipv6 router isis`)
- Say when single-topology IS-IS black-holes IPv6, and why multi-topology IS-IS (RFC 5120) plus `metric-style wide` exists
- Place RFC 5838 (OSPFv3 address families, including IPv4) and RFC 7166 (authentication trailer) in that picture
- Pick a dual-stack IGP approach for a lab without declaring a universal winner

**Version note.** FRR, netlab, and containerlab were not installed and were not run on the writing host (2026-11-13, Linux 6.12.94+). Every FRR snippet, `show` command, and netlab topology below is written from the FRR ospf6d / isisd documentation, the cited RFCs, and netlab.tools, and is **illustrative**.

## Two protocols, or one process with two topologies

```text
  IPv4-only IGP                  Dual-stack choices
  -------------                  ------------------
  OSPFv2  ─────────────┬───────► OSPFv2  +  OSPFv3     (two LSDB, two adjacencies)
                       │
                       └───────► IS-IS, IPv4 + IPv6
                                   ├─ single topology (one SPF for both)
                                   └─ multi-topology  (RFC 5120: e.g. ipv6-unicast SPF)
```

OSPFv3 began as the IPv6-only counterpart of OSPFv2 (RFC 2740, updated by RFC 5340). You run it as a separate process, with its own LSDB and its own adjacencies, even on a link that already has OSPFv2. RFC 5838 later added *address-family* support so an OSPFv3 process can also carry IPv4; that is the modern option, not the historical default, and not every lab image will be configured for it.

IS-IS started as an ISO IGP and grew IPv4 reachability (RFC 1195) and then IPv6 reachability (RFC 5308) as TLVs in the same LSP. One adjacency, one flooding machine, optionally one SPF — or, with multi-topology, a second SPF for IPv6 so an IPv4-only neighbor does not drag IPv6 down.

## OSPFv3: what actually changed

A few properties surprise people who treat OSPFv3 as a paint job.

**Router ID is still 32 bits.** It is written as a dotted quad (`192.0.2.1`) and is *not* an IPv6 address. On an IPv6-only box there may be no IPv4 address to derive it from, so you configure it. FRR: `ospf6 router-id A.B.C.D`. If you change it, FRR documents `clear ipv6 ospf6 process` rather than “just restart later and hope.”

**Hellos go to IPv6 multicast, from a link-local source.** All-SPF-Routers is `FF02::5`, All-DRouters `FF02::6`. The adjacency is built with link-local addresses. Global or ULA addresses on the interface are not required for OSPFv3 signalling, and FRR’s own documentation is blunt that there is no OSPFv3 reason to put them on the interface if you do not otherwise need them.

**Interface IPv6 prefixes are not in the hello the way OSPFv2 carried IPv4 addresses.** Prefixes travel in Intra-Area-Prefix LSAs (and Link LSAs for on-link information). That split is why you can have a working adjacency and still be missing a prefix: the neighbor is up, the LSA type is different.

**Instance ID exists.** Multiple OSPFv3 instances can share a link. FRR’s interface sample uses `ipv6 ospf6 instance-id 0`. Mismatched instance IDs do not form an adjacency.

**Areas, costs, DR/BDR, stubs and NSSAs are still there.** The IPv4 OSPF chapter’s mental model of areas and types still applies. FRR’s `ipv6 ospf6 area`, `ipv6 ospf6 cost`, hello/dead/retransmit, and `area … range` / NSSA commands are the IPv6-named counterparts. PtP vs broadcast is still a configuration choice; FRR does not support NBMA for IPv6 and says it likely never will.

**Authentication is not “use IPsec or go home.”** The original OSPFv3 text assumed IPsec. RFC 7166 defines an authentication trailer. FRR supports it as `ipv6 ospf6 authentication` with a manual key (MD5 or HMAC-SHA-256 in the internal crypto build; more algorithms with OpenSSL) or a keychain. Do not write “OSPFv3 has no authentication.”

### FRR shape (illustrative)

From the FRR ospf6d documentation, a one-interface, one-area process looks like this:

```frr
interface eth0
 ipv6 ospf6 area 0.0.0.0
 ipv6 ospf6 instance-id 0
!
router ospf6
 ospf6 router-id 192.0.2.1
 area 0.0.0.0 range 2001:db8:105:2::/64
!
```

Enable it on every interface that should participate, including a loopback if you want that prefix in the area (loopbacks are often point-to-point / passive, as in OSPFv2). Useful show commands, also illustrative:

```text
show ipv6 ospf6
show ipv6 ospf6 neighbor
show ipv6 ospf6 route
show ipv6 ospf6 interface
```

A later lab-host-track IPv6 lab is where you would paste real output from cEOS or FRR. Nothing here was executed.

## IS-IS for IPv6: TLVs, then multi-topology

RFC 5308 adds two TLVs: **IPv6 Reachability** (prefixes, metric, up/down and external bits) and **IPv6 Interface Address**. IPv6 IS-IS uses the same levels, the same LSP flooding, and the same NET as IPv4 IS-IS. On FRR you attach IPv6 to an already-defined process with an interface command, not a second NET:

```frr
interface eth0
 ip router isis CORE
 ipv6 router isis CORE
!
router isis CORE
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 metric-style wide
!
```

`ip router isis` is IPv4 on that interface; `ipv6 router isis` is IPv6. The process name (`CORE`) must match `router isis`. Other platforms (for example some EOS-style CLIs) enable the IPv6 address-family under the IS-IS process instead of on the interface. Believe the image you are running.

### Single topology is the trap

If IPv4 and IPv6 share one topology, they share one SPF. A neighbor that is IPv4-only, or a link that has IPv4 but no IPv6, still sits in that graph. IPv6 prefixes can be advertised with a next hop or a path that cannot forward IPv6, or an IPv6-only island can look closer than it is. The failure is quiet: the IPv4 adjacency is up, IPv6 routes appear, packets do not.

**Multi-topology IS-IS (RFC 5120)** gives IPv6 its own topology identifier and its own SPF. A router without IPv6 on a link simply does not participate in the IPv6 topology on that link. FRR enables this under the process:

```frr
router isis CORE
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 metric-style wide
 topology ipv6-unicast
```

FRR requires **wide metrics** when any multi-topology is configured. `metric-style narrow` with `topology ipv6-unicast` is a configuration error (the daemon will refuse it). Enable MT on every router that should agree on the IPv6 graph; a mixed MT / single-topology area is not a lab you will enjoy debugging.

With MT, a three-router line where the third router has no IPv6 toward the others will still have IPv4 reachability to all three loopbacks, and IPv6 reachability only where the IPv6 topology is actually connected. That is the behaviour you want, and the reason to turn MT on in a dual-stack lab before the topology gets interesting.

## Which one should a dual-stack lab use?

There is no single right answer. The useful trade-offs are:

| Approach | You gain | You pay |
|----------|----------|---------|
| OSPFv2 + OSPFv3 | Familiar IPv4 OSPF stays untouched; IPv6 is a second, well-understood protocol | Two processes, two LSDBs, two authentications, two places a link can be in the wrong area |
| OSPFv3 with RFC 5838 AFs | One OSPFv3 process can carry IPv6 and IPv4 | Support and default config vary; do not assume the image is in AF mode |
| IS-IS, single topology | One adjacency, one set of LSPs | IPv4-only or IPv6-only links can black-hole the other family |
| IS-IS, multi-topology | One adjacency and flooding, separate SPFs | Wide metrics, MT on every speaker, a slightly larger mental model |

A network that already runs OSPFv2 often adds OSPFv3 rather than introducing IS-IS only to get IPv6. A network that already runs IS-IS, or a green-field dual-stack core, often prefers one IS-IS process with `topology ipv6-unicast`. In this book’s labs, pick one approach and keep it consistent across the topology.

## A netlab sketch (illustrative, not run)

netlab will configure OSPF or IS-IS from the corresponding module once the nodes have IPv6 addresses. A three-router dual-stack triangle, still just YAML, might look like this (check your netlab version’s OSPF/IS-IS module pages for exact IPv6 / MT attributes before you rely on a flag name):

```yaml
# illustrative — not executed; confirm module knobs with netlab.tools
defaults.device: frr
addressing.p2p.ipv6: 2001:db8:0:1::/64

module: [ ospf ]
# or: module: [ isis ]  and an isis area/NET, plus IPv6 / MT if the module supports it

nodes:
  r1:
  r2:
  r3:

links:
  - r1-r2
  - r2-r3
  - r1-r3
```

For OSPF, expect OSPFv2 for IPv4 and OSPFv3 for IPv6 unless you have deliberately chosen an AF mode the image supports. For IS-IS, expect a single process; enable IPv6 and multi-topology explicitly rather than hoping the default matches RFC 5120. `netlab report` and `netlab validate` are the same loop as in the BGP and modules chapters; no report was generated here.

## Gotchas

- **Forgetting the OSPFv3 router ID on an IPv6-only box.** The process may not come up the way you expect, or it may pick an ID you did not plan for. Set it.
- **Filtering ICMPv6 and “allowing OSPF.”** OSPFv3 is ICMPv6-adjacent in the operator’s mind but it is its own protocol (89) on IPv6. Also do not filter the link-local traffic it uses to hello.
- **Single-topology IS-IS on a mixed IPv4/IPv6 graph.** The adjacency is not a guarantee that IPv6 follows IPv4.
- **Narrow metrics plus MT in FRR.** The daemon should reject it; if you pasted a snippet from an IPv4-only lab, this is why.
- **Assuming OSPFv3 has no authentication.** RFC 7166 and FRR’s `ipv6 ospf6 authentication` exist. Use them in any lab that is not a closed netns.
- **Pinging a prefix that the IGP advertised from a loopback /128 or a discard.** Reachability of a prefix and presence in the LSDB are different checks.

## Boring rule

Treat IPv6 as a first-class topology, not a second address on an IPv4 IGP. Either run OSPFv3 properly (router ID, link-local, prefixes in the right LSAs) or run IS-IS with an IPv6 topology you can draw, preferably multi-topology.

## Try this

1. On a three-router FRR lab, bring up OSPFv3 only, with a manually set router ID, and write down `show ipv6 ospf6 neighbor` and `show ipv6 ospf6 route` (your output, not this chapter’s).
2. Convert the same graph to IS-IS with `ipv6 router isis` but *without* MT, then shut IPv6 on one link and predict which IPv6 loopbacks disappear — or worse, remain with a useless next hop.
3. Enable `metric-style wide` and `topology ipv6-unicast` on all three and repeat the shutdown. The IPv4 graph should stay, the IPv6 graph should look like the remaining IPv6 links.
4. Add RFC 7166 authentication on one OSPFv3 link and confirm the adjacency dies until both sides match.
